summary: Specifies how to authenticate PIM-SM link-local messages with IPsec ESP, or optionally AH, and how to add confidentiality with ESP. Manual keying is the mandatory default, with other mechanisms considered for scalability and security. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Neighboring routers put a seal on the notes they pass to each other, so fake notes from an imposter get ignored.

questions: how to secure pim-sm hello messages
how to authenticate pim hello messages
does pim-sm require esp or ah
subtitle: How PIM-SM routers use IPsec to prove that link-local control messages really come from their neighbors.

tldr.problem: PIM-SM routers send Hello, Join/Prune and Assert messages to a shared multicast address on each link, so an attacker on the link can forge them and disturb the multicast distribution tree.
tldr.mechanism: Each message is protected with IPsec: ESP is mandatory and AH is optional, with HMAC-SHA1 for authentication and optional AES-CBC encryption. Manual keying is the mandatory default, with automated group key management left to other documents.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5796 updates RFC 4601 and is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted. It gives implementers a concrete recipe, but manual keys have known drawbacks.

today: RFC 5796 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4601. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem: Forged Link-Local Messages
sections.content:
All PIM-SM control messages use IP protocol number 103. Some are unicast. The rest are multicast with a TTL of 1 to the address ALL_PIM_ROUTERS (224.0.0.13 in IPv4 and ff02::d in IPv6), using a link-local source address. These are the link-local messages, and they include Hello, Join/Prune and Assert.

A forged link-local message sent to ALL_PIM_ROUTERS by an attacker affects the construction of the distribution tree. RFC 4601 describes the effects, some severe and some minor. RFC 5796 updates RFC 4601 so that its security text lines up with the newer AH and ESP specifications. Unicast PIM messages are not the focus, because a normal unicast IPsec Security Association (SA) already covers them.

The primary goal is data origin authentication of each link-local message. A secondary goal is that only legitimate adjacent routers talk to each other. An optional goal is confidentiality. Giving each router a unique identity is assumed, but how to create one is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Routers shout hellos and instructions to everyone on their street. Without a seal, a stranger could shout fake instructions and confuse them, so this document says how to add a seal.

sections.title: Authentication, Confidentiality and Modes
sections.content:
Conforming implementations MUST support SAs in transport mode. They MAY also support tunnel mode, and if they do, both destination and source address preservation MUST be used.

Authentication MUST be supported, with ESP required and AH optional. Implementations MUST support HMAC-SHA1. ESP in transport mode authenticates the PIM-SM packet but not the IP header, extension headers or options. AH in transport mode also covers selected portions of those. Packets that lack protection, or fail the checks, are silently discarded by IPsec, although a counter may be kept.

Confidentiality is a SHOULD. If provided, ESP MUST be used with AES-CBC and a 128-bit key. An implementation MUST NOT generate the combination of non-NULL encryption and NULL authentication.
sections.eli5: Every note must carry a seal that proves who wrote it. Hiding what the note says is a nice extra, but the seal is the must-have.

sections.title: Required IPsec Capabilities
sections.content:
The IPsec implementation under the router needs several features. It MUST support multiple Security Policy Databases (SPDs), with a way to pick one by interface. It MUST be able to use source address, destination address, protocol and direction as selectors, and to tag inbound packets with the ID of the interface they arrived on. Manually configured keys MUST be possible.

The algorithm requirements of RFC 4835 apply. Implementations MUST support ESP-NULL, and MUST NOT let the user pick a stream cipher or counter-mode block cipher with manual keys. IP encapsulation of ESP MUST be supported, and UDP encapsulation SHOULD NOT be used.

If automated keying is implemented, the implementation also MUST support the Group Security Policy Database (GSPD) from RFC 5374, multiple GSPDs chosen by interface, and the same selectors.
sections.eli5: A router needs a few special tools in its toolbox to make and check the seals, including a way to remember which street each note came in from.

sections.title: Key Management and Security Associations
sections.content:
All implementations MUST support manual configuration of the SAs. This does not rule out a negotiation protocol such as GDOI (RFC 3547) or GSAKMP (RFC 4535). Manual keying is workable when the number of directly connected routers is small. The administrator enters the SA parameters and configures the SPD so the SA is used when sending.

Link-local messages go to a single multicast address, so each speaking router is effectively the center of a small group made up of its neighbors. A listening router must tell its neighbors apart, since each has its own sequence-number space. Link-local addresses are unique only per interface, so the interface ID tag is needed as an extra selector.

The RFC describes two ways to arrange SAs. In the first, each node uses a unique SA for outbound traffic, which should be supported by every implementation and scales well with automated keying. In the second, all nodes use two SAs, one for sending (SAo) and one for receiving (SAi), with identical parameters across the region. The second method MUST be supported and is recommended for manual configuration.

The procedures for automated key management are not specified here. GDOI and GSAKMP are named as options.
sections.eli5: Everyone on the street can share one secret seal stamp, which is easy but risky, or each neighbor can have their own stamp, which is safer but needs more bookkeeping.

sections.title: Rekeying Without Dropping Messages
sections.content:
Keys SHOULD be changed periodically, and also when trusted personnel change. The encryption and authentication keys SHOULD be changed at least every 90 days. The RFC admits that automated key management would remove the drawbacks of manual keys, but suitable techniques did not yet exist, so implementations MUST support manual rekeying.

The three-step procedure keeps the adjacency alive:

  1. On every router on the link, add an extra inbound SA with a new SPI and key.
  2. On every router, replace the outbound SA with one using the new SPI and key. This swap MUST be atomic so no PIM-SM packet goes out unprotected.
  3. On every router, remove the original inbound SA.

All routers MUST finish a step before any starts the next. A configurable KeyRolloverInterval can pace this: a router waits that long after starting a step before moving on. All routers on a link MUST use the same value, and the administrator chooses it.
sections.eli5: To swap the secret stamp, everyone first learns to read the new seal, then everyone starts using it, and only then does everyone forget the old one. Nobody gets left out.

sections.title: SA Lookup, Anti-Replay and Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
A receiving router MUST look up the SA using the SPI, the destination address and the sender address. Because sender addresses may be only locally unique, the interface ID tag, the SPI and the sender address MUST all be used. In effect, link-local communication is source-specific multicast that happens to use a shared any-source multicast address.

This lookup splits the multi-sender group into separate single-sender associations, so the AH note that anti-replay is unavailable for a multi-sender SA does not matter here. Anti-replay is RECOMMENDED only when SAs come from automated key management. With manual keys it SHOULD NOT be activated. A sender's sequence-number counter MUST be maintained across reboots until the key is replaced.

With manual keys, the 64-bit Extended Sequence Number (ESN) SHOULD be used, since a PIM router can never exhaust it. A manually keyed SA using ESN MUST save it, with an indication of which sequence numbers were used, over a reboot.
sections.eli5: When a note arrives, the router checks which neighbor and which street it came from before picking the matching seal to check.

sections.title: Limits of Manual Keys
sections.content:
The RFC lists known limitations of manual keys. Without replay protection, routers are not secured against attacks that replay PIM packets. Manual keys are usually long lived, giving an attacker time to find them. Administrators may also pick weak keys.

Using the same key on all routers on a link leaves all of them open to impersonation if any one router is compromised, malfunctioning or misconfigured. For more analysis the RFC points to RFC 4593, RFC 5294, RFC 4609 and the security section of RFC 4601.
sections.eli5: If everybody shares one stamp and one neighbor loses it, a stranger can fake notes from anyone. That is why changing the stamp often matters.
